messages.subject: scantwo issue due to large vector size
messages.subject_clean: scantwo issue due to large vector size
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to run scantwo using Drosophila recombinant inbred lines, I have 256 lines and 6624 markers. When I try to run scantwo I encounter a problem with the vector being too large (~13.2GB), and from what I was able to find it seems like R itself only handle vectors up to 8GB. I tried to downsize my data set by droping whole chromosome arms and went down to 1239 markers, but the vector produced by scantwo didn't reduce in size at all.

I was surprised that reducing the number of markers didn't have an effect on vector size. When I calculate genotype probabilities I am using step size 0, since the data set is already dense. Are there options to try to avoid having this issue and use scantwo or should I just try a different approach on my mapping experiment? My next attempt would be to perform multi-QTL.

example code:
> ril_gp <- calc.genoprob(ril_data,step=0, err=0.001)
> etoh_s2 <- scantwo( ril_gp   , verbose = FALSE, method="em")

Thanks in advance for any help.

Best,
--

Best,

messages.body_plain:
In reducing from 6624 markers to 1239, you're going down by a factor of 5, so the requested vector size from scantwo should go down by a factor of 25.
The 1239 marker case should be do-able. You'd probably want to use method="hk" rather than method="em", for speed.

I'm kind of surprised that you can't do 6624 markers. I'd have thought it would use more like 6624*6624*8 bytes = about 350 MB.

karl

messages.subject: QTL peak moves around
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,
I have encountered a problem where a QTL peak jumps around when I re-run with the same input and code.
I have two data sets that come from a biparental inbred wheat population. The first data set has less genetic resolution (doubled-haploid), 162 individuals, ~1,500 markers distributed evenly across 21 chromosomes, 99.3% genotyped, and ~90% phenotyped (BLUP across 6 site-year observations). We used this data, and the following code to identify a QTL for the phenotype TGW:

SynOpData <- calc.genoprob(SynOpDH_phys, step = 0, map.function = "kosambi")
TGW_BLUP <- cim(SynOpData, pheno.col = "BLUP_TGW", method = "hk")

Based on the QTL we found for TGW we developed inbred lines selecting for recombination events within the flanking markers (~50 Mbp) in order to fine-map. This data set has only 33 markers, 31 of which are on the chromosome with the QTL and 2 are another chromosome that also has a QTL for TGW (129 individuals, 4 site-year observations, 99% genotyped, 99% phenotyped). When I run the following code I get narrow peaks (<10 Mbp) for the QTL, but the can jump around, for example from peak at 341 Mbp to peak at 380 Mbp, and they always remain significant (LOD ~30):

SynOpData <- calc.genoprob(SynOpHIF, step = 0, map.function = "kosambi")
TGW_BLUP <- cim(SynOpData, pheno.col = "TGW_BLUP", method = "hk")

Alternatively when I remove the two markers on the other chromosome and run:
SynOpData <- calc.genoprob(SynOpHIF, step = 0, map.function = "kosambi")
TGW_BLUP <- scanone(SynOpData, pheno.col = "TGW_BLUP", method = "hk")

the QTL does not jump around but the peaks remain significant with far less resolution, two peaks at both 341 and 380 Mbp (LOD ~ 30) and the markers in-between have LOD > 10.

I understand there may be two peaks for two different genes but I don't understand why the QTL moves so dramatically re-running the same code with cim(). Should I not use cim() for a dataset with that few of markers? It is strange that we can reproduce the peaks in the first dataset with cim(). Any help would be greatly appreciated.
Cheers,
Ellie

messages.subject: Re: QTL peak moves around
messages.body_plain:
cim() first does forward selection to choose a set of marker covariates; this requires complete data at the markers, and so any missing genotypes are filled in by a single random imputation. That's likely the cause of the changes.

I recommend against using cim(); it would generally be better to use stepwiseqtl() or the MQM functions.

karl

messages.subject: best practices for non-normal phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Hello R/qtl pros,

I am working on a project exploring the genetic architecture of 14 floral traits related to pollination syndromes. In my F2 population, phenotypes of five of these traits are normally distributed, and the rest are not. I am looking for some advice in terms of best practices when analyzing a dataset like this. Is transforming the non-normal phenotype data the way to go? Because if I don't, I can only go as far as scanone with model=np, correct? It would be ideal to be able to do the stepwiseqtl analyses for all traits, not just the normally distributed ones.

Many thanks for your help!

Molly

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] best practices for non-normal phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Molly,

We routinely transform (quantile normalization) all our phenotype data (except binomially distributed data) prior to using the stepwise procedure. You can then refit the QTL model using the untransformed data to get allelic effect sizes that are in units of the phenotype.

I'm sure others will have potentially better solutions, but this is what works for me.

Take care,

Chris

I have a couple of follow up questions, as you have time.
I'm working with DHs and RILs, and have been using `convert2riself()` for the cross, but stepwiseqtl() does not like this population structure. I also tried BC.gen = 0, F.gen = 6, as a workaround but that didn't work either. Do you have any advice for inbreds and stepwiseqtl?

Thank you for your guidance.
Cheers,
Ellie

messages.subject: Re: QTL peak moves around
messages.body_plain:
I expect the problem you have concerns the fact that stepwiseqtl() has default penalties for a backcross or intercross only. But these are based on simulations for the mouse genome with markers at a 10 cM spacing, and so I wouldn't recommend using these. Rather, you would use simulations or a permutation test to derive these for your cross and genome.

I think the apparent 10 cM resolution of QTL location from cim() is not real but is due to the windowing approach. If you increase the window size to 20 you'd probably see the QTL regions widen. This is one of the reasons that I don't generally like using cim.

karl

messages.body_plain:
If you're just going to look for additive QTL (ignoring interactions), then you just need a "main effect" penalty, which you can get from scanone() permutation.

operm <- scanone(mycross, method="hk", n.perm=1000)
threshold <- summary(operm, 0.05)

You'd then use:

out <- stepwiseqtl(mycross, method="hk", penalties=threshold, additive.only=TRUE)

If you also want to consider interactions, you need to penalties with a two-dimensional scan. Best to use the function scantwopermhk(), but even the it will be extremely computationally intensive and you probably want to use a computer cluster.
With the scantwo permutation results, you'd use calc.penalties() to get the penalties.

karl

I would probably not transform any of these. The skew of spur curvature and total nector might suggest square-root or logs, but they're really not so bad. The bimodal distributions particularly of sepal CIELAB a* and b* may suggest a major QTL and you don't want to transform that away. (It's not the phenotype distribution itself that needs to be normal, but the residual variation).

The ideas others have suggested (taking logs or normal quantiles) are good. The question of what to do with non-normal phenotype distributions in QTL mapping is the same as the question of what to do with non-normally distributed outcomes in multiple linear regression. Generally linear regression is quite robust, and non-constant residual variance is a bigger problem than non-normality.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I used a double digestion sequencing approach to get SNP markers for 350 progeny (F1 generation). The genome size is 20MB and there are 14 chromosomes. After I removed distorted markers, cosegregating markers, as well as consolidate markers within 500bp of each other, I ended up with about 1119 markers. est.map(mydata,error.prob=.01,map.function="kosambi",maxit=100000)

I think I have some problems here.
There are many large gaps, most obvious one is on chromosome 7, which has a gap of 46 cM. I checked the markers here and found they do have a large physical distance apart from each other (over 50kb, the average kb per centimorgan is 5kb). I checked recombination frequency myself and did find it is about 40%.
My total cM sizes of chromosomes are over 100, and chromosome 1 is about 200 centimorgans. I am wondering why and how I can improve them. The greatest recombination frequency can only be 50%, so I think I should not have chromosomes which are as big as 200cM.

Thank you anyone for your suggestions or help.

Sincerely,
Ben Chadwick

messages.subject: stepwise qtl conundra
messages.body_plain:
Hi team,

I could use some advice regarding my stepwise analyses.

First, a very basic question about how the penalties are working. The main effect penalty derived from 1000 permutations on most of my traits winds up being around 3.4. I thought that the stepwise scan would select a model with the highest LOD only if that LOD was 3.4 higher than the previous model, but got confused when I saw the map output and the pLODs weren't increasing by 3.4. Just wanted to double-check that if I see a pLOD increase from 42.5 to 45 from one model to the next, this increase is 2.5 *over* the penalty of 3.4?

I ask this because sometimes the stepwise scan divides a single large peak into two small tightly linked peaks (with drastically lower lods and PVEs) so that the overall pLOD can improve from 45.64 to 46.25, for example. I'm not sure that this added complexity in the model is actually 'worth' the very small improvement, or if it makes biological sense in the context of this trait and system. Are there other ways to assess model improvement?

This leads to a more general best practices question - how should we be choosing the maximum number of QTL for stepwise scans? I know that picking a huge number of QTL is a no-no because it will result in noise/overfitting. I had tried choosing based on the number of peaks produced by scanone and scantwo plus one or two extra just in case (especially when the scanone results looked like there were two distinct peaks at either end of a chromosome, for example), but this is leading to results like the one above or producing very small peaks that were never detected by scanone and scantwo. In other words, if I pick maximum qtl = number of peaks from scanone, I worry that I will miss instances where peaks *should* be divided up; but if I pick maximum qtl > number of peaks from scanone it seems like sometimes it results in overfitting. Would a compromise be to go with the number from scanone, but in cases where I think I see two peaks in scanone, go back and add qtl and assess improvement?

Many thanks in advance for your qtl wisdom!

Molly

messages.body_plain:
The penalized LOD, pLOD, is LOD - penalty x number of QTL
The LOD score needs to go up by at least the penalty before you would add another QTL.

See Broman & Speed 2002 and Manichakul et al 2009 for details
https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00354
https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.108.094565

What to use as maximum number of QTL? I think avoid getting near a model with more than like n/5 parameters. But otherwise I’d feel free to try increasing the value and see if you get a better-supported model, in terms of pLOD.

karl

messages.body_plain:
If you have a QTL with super strong effect, as seems to be the case here, use of the genotype probabilities may not fully account for the effect of the locus, and so if using Haley-Knott regression, it may seem like there’s evidence for multiple tightly linked QTL in a region.

One approach is to do a single imputation at the inferred QTL, and use those inferred genotypes as a covariate. For example, use fill.geno() and then pull.geno() and then pull out the appropriate column.

karl

messages.subject: two-stage analyses
messages.body_plain:
Hi R/qtl group;

I’m emailing to get your opinion on a few analysis
ideas.  I’m especially interested in
hearing your thoughts and opinions about the use of “multiple stage” approaches
to increase power in mapping.  We’ve been
doing QTL and GWAS mapping in plants for many years. One thing that has always
been a focus is doing our best to control background genetic and environmental
effects to increase our power. We’ve used multiple QTL models, and more recently
models with polygenic terms, to control for segregating QTL.  In terms of environmental effects, we’ll
often include covariates associated with the experimental design like blocks,
benches, trays, or even x y spatial coordinates.  These analyses are often completed first –
followed by a secondary analysis in Rqtl based on the residuals, lsmeans, or
blups from a prior statistical analysis. In a similar vein, we usually complete QTL
mapping using RIL means determined from a first stage analysis (and leaving behind
the within RIL variance).

Several of our recent projects have utilized unreplicated
plantings of experimental crosses or outbred GWAS panels.  In these cases, we have a single
plant/genotype that has been phenotyped, sequenced, and planted in a grid with other
unreplicated genotypes and some “checks” (replicated controls) in the field.
 For mapping studies, this is fine as we can think of the unit of
replication as the allele and can simply run our mapping as you would for an unreplicated
F2 or a human GWAS study. However, we’d still like to calculate variance components
and h2 (commonly reported for quantitative genetic studies) as well as control
for environmental variance when possible. Recently, we’ve used linear mixed
models and a relationship matrix to partition Va, Ve, and to estimate narrow-sense
heritability in these unreplicated studies. We can also get “blup” estimates of
the breeding values from these models.  My
question is whether it is appropriate or valid to use the blups based on
kinship in subsequent genetic mapping analyses. We’ve tried this and see marked
increase in LOD scores and often detect many more QTL. On the one hand, I’d
expect this as we should see an increase in power by reducing Ve and focusing on genetic values, especially for traits with relatively low h2. However, I’m a
bit concerned that it’s circular in that the markers are used to estimate
kinship from the first stage and used again in the mapping.  It might not be
a terrible concern because the markers are used in aggregate for the kinship
based mixed model and probably aren’t predictive of any single genotype in the
mapping analysis. However, I’m old enough to be concerned when things look
too good to be true.

Has anyone seen this type of two-staged analysis?  Do you think the use of a marker-based kinship to estimate breeding values will create bias or problems with subsequent
mapping?

I’ve love to hear your thoughts,

Best,

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

I'm influenced by Hans-Peter Piepho who is definitely against BLUPing the BLUPs, and has published to this effect I think. This is more for GWAS than linkage analysis, but I guess similar arguments apply. Can you use weighted BLUEs in the second stage instead? You would then map these with a kinship matrix plus testing individual markers as fixed effects. I think that's what Hans-Peter would do. Against that, if you use empirical significance thresholds for your mapping, should it matter that much what you do?

Best wishes,

Ian
